posts.text: So what does it mean that Claude can write these scenes and fool most people? Well it doesn’t mean writers will be replaced. One thing I always consider re: AI is that humans haven’t been able to reliably beat computers in chess in decades but chess is wildly popular now.

(One of the funniest tells was fidgeting. Claude kept having characters run a finger along a table’s edge or touch their neck or whatever else. This was most of the action. Again, it’s bc we also write prose where ppl are always running their fingers along a tables edge)

But the dead scenes persisted. And while it’s tempting to say Claude’s great tell is that it only writes dead scenes w empty hallways and ppl saying nothing, it makes those choices bc we, as writers, are also always writing scenes filled with detail and style and quiet.

This was enough to make the game a coin flip. Tens of thousands of rounds were played and ppl correctly guessed ‘real’ or ‘fake’ at a stubborn 51%. So Claude in some ways had succeeded in convincing the players that a passage it had written was Sherwood Anderson or Joyce.

I also noticed it wasn’t exactly capturing the style and so I asked it to try to do a better job. The solution it came up with was to write ‘cards’ and assign another robot to check for tells and style pointers. Here are some of the cards it generated.

In this passage, every sentence is either someone doing nothing, having no reaction, not comprehending someone else, or saying nothing. 

Why do the robots write such inert scenes? Well, because humans tend to write scenes like this. 

I tried to just have Claude write action…

The obvious tells eventually went away and most of the ppl playing the game were just flipping a coin. (A small percentage were actually good at it.)

But there was one persistent tell. Claude kept writing scenes where the characters did nothing.

I made this game and did a bunch of testing rounds while tinkering with how a few LLMs reproduced public domain works of literature. I gave it lists of ‘tells’ to avoid like em dashes, similes, (AI is particularly bad at these), vague words.

my upcoming book about panicking parents, youth sports, schools, safetyism, and technology now has a page and a cover.

The book is a confession/convo about being a crazy sports dad, myself, and how parenting got so intensely privatized. 

penguinrandomhouse.com/books…

some topics discussed: public school curricula, the pandemic, pick up and drop off circles, Kumon, and much more. Please pre-order the book. Will keep you all updated as we get towards publication day.

I wrote the book as a coming together of frustrated parents in a Chautauqua-styled conversation to talk about what is great about parenting (like watching your kid compete and score goals) and how we can get back to a sane, healthy version of that.
